data: Religion and Society in South Asia

This course is about the study of Religion with a particular focus on South Asian religions (Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, Zorastrianism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism), as they have been studied anthropologically, historically and politically – as daily beliefs and practices, and in relation to wider South Asian culture, history and politics. This course will provide both a grounded study of religious practices and religions in Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, Sikkim, Sri Lanka as well as a postcolonial critique of the study of religions and nationalism in the South Asian realm.
The course will explore why the transformation of the public sphere in South Asia shows the increasing importance of religious movements, and of the political use of religious symbolism in new communication technologies. One of the most important trends in the present era is the attempt to create a homogenous religious community, not only within the national territorial space, but also in a transnational space. If such attempts offer a sense of identity for communities, it also offers a brutal confrontation with “the Other,” however defined. The violent conflicts between Hindus and Muslims, between “high” castes and Dalits, between Shi’as and Sunnis, between Buddhists and Hindus, Buddhists and Muslims are sad reminders of a growing confrontation which is not only regional, but increasingly global.
This course will therefore combine historical awareness, conceptual acuity, spatial mobility. This will lead us to an analysis of the effects of imperial interactions, state formation and how these provide a crucial perspective for the unravelling of the multiple transformations of religion, religious nationalisms, the global framework of religious fraternities, and what informs the choice of certain identities over others.
